precepts.text: Lot dwelt in Sodom; pitching toward Sodom ended with dwelling in it.
precepts.point: The men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the Lord exceedingly: they were lawless, without principles, and given to sexual freedom. That is why the city was overthrown.

note.label: Genesis 13: The Peacemaker and the Promise

precepts.why:
Lot “pitched his tent toward Sodom.” One chapter later, when the kings came against the cities of the plain, “they took Lot, Abram’s brother’s son, who dwelt in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.” Toward Sodom became in Sodom.

Lot lifted up his eyes and chose the plain of Jordan because it was well watered every where, fertile “as the garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt.” But “the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the Lord exceedingly”: lawless, without principles, and given to sexual freedom. That is why the city was overthrown.

He pitched toward that city, and he ended up dwelling in it, and he was carried away captive with it. That is where pitching toward Sodom leads.

precepts.text: It is no hard matter for many to be shut up in the hands of a few; the victory of battle standeth not in the multitude of an host.
precepts.point: The victory of battle stands not in the multitude of an host; strength comes from heaven. Whether with many or with them that have no power, the battle is not yours but God's; our forefathers proved it, as when Asa cried to the Lord and a million Ethiopians fell before Judah and Benjamin.

note.label: Genesis 14: The War of the Kings and Melchizedek

precepts.why:
Abram went against four kingdoms with “his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen”, and his three confederates, Mamre, Eshcol and Aner. He divided his men and moved by night; that is military strategy. Abram trained those servants himself: he was a warrior fit for battle who knew how to conduct war, nothing like the frail figure in the whitewashed images.

Judas said it: “It is no hard matter for many to be shut up in the hands of a few; and with the God of heaven it is all one, to deliver with a great multitude, or a small company: For the victory of battle standeth not in the multitude of an host; but strength cometh from heaven.”

That is how three hundred and eighteen men smote four kingdoms and brought back Lot, the goods, the women and the people. The victory was not in the numbers; the strength came from heaven.

precepts.text: Be not afraid by reason of this great multitude; the battle is not yours, but God's.
precepts.point: The victory of battle stands not in the multitude of an host; strength comes from heaven. Whether with many or with them that have no power, the battle is not yours but God's; our forefathers proved it, as when Asa cried to the Lord and a million Ethiopians fell before Judah and Benjamin.

note.label: Genesis 14: The War of the Kings and Melchizedek

precepts.why:
The word to Judah facing a great multitude is the word behind Abram’s victory: “Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s.”

Abram “heard that his brother was taken captive” and went after four kings with three hundred and eighteen trained servants. Whether with many or with few, the battle is not yours but God’s, and that is why he smote them and “brought back all the goods, and also brought again his brother Lot.”

precepts.text: Asa rested on the Lord against a thousand thousand Ethiopians; it is nothing with the Lord to help, whether with many or with them that have no power.
precepts.point: The victory of battle stands not in the multitude of an host; strength comes from heaven. Whether with many or with them that have no power, the battle is not yours but God's; our forefathers proved it, as when Asa cried to the Lord and a million Ethiopians fell before Judah and Benjamin.

note.label: Genesis 14: The War of the Kings and Melchizedek

precepts.why:
Our forefathers proved that strength comes from heaven. Zerah the Ethiopian came out against Asa “with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots”, a million men. Asa set the battle in array and cried unto the Lord his God: “Lord, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O Lord our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude.”

A million Ethiopians fell before Judah and Benjamin. It is nothing with the Lord to help, whether with many or with them that have no power.

That is the same Lord Abram rested on when he took three hundred and eighteen men and three confederates against four kingdoms and smote them by night. The victory of battle stands not in the multitude of an host; “let not man prevail against thee.”

precepts.text: After the war Abram told the king of Sodom, I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich; the Most High was his provider, and that is the spirit of the forefathers.
precepts.point: Laban agreed, then removed that same day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, all the speckled and spotted she goats, and the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his own sons, setting three days' journey between himself and Jacob.

note.label: Genesis 30: Trouble in the Flesh and a Righteous Hire

precepts.why:
After the war, “the king of Sodom said unto Abram, Give me the persons, and take the goods to thyself.” Abram refused: “I have lift up mine hand unto the Lord, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth, That I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, and that I will not take any thing that is thine, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich”. The Most High was his provider, and no man was going to say he made Abram rich.

Jacob has the same spirit when Laban asks, “What shall I give thee?” “Thou shalt not give me any thing”. He asked no gift, only terms: he would keep feeding Laban's flock, and the speckled, spotted and brown among the sheep and goats from that day forward would be his hire. And he set terms that could be checked in the open: “So shall my righteousness answer for me in time to come”, and every one that was not speckled and spotted among the goats and brown among the sheep would “be counted stolen with me.” Judge me on my works; my word is my bond. He said it because he knew they were going to have something bad to say about his increase.

That refusal is the spirit our forefathers rolled in, Abram and Jacob alike. We have to come back to these scriptures and to the understanding of who we are, because our people are lost and have fainted from that spirit. We cannot roll in a handout spirit; when we repent we have to conduct ourselves as men and provide for our own houses, for the Most High provides.

precepts.text: The Horites were in their mount Seir already in Abraham's day.
precepts.point: The Lord destroyed the Horims from before the children of Esau, and they succeeded them and dwelt in their stead, as Deuteronomy records.

note.label: Genesis 36: The Generations of Esau, Who Is Edom

precepts.why:
“And the Horites in their mount Seir, unto El–paran, which is by the wilderness.” In Abraham's day the Horites were already in their mount Seir.

That is why Genesis 36 lists “the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land”, with their dukes “in the land of Edom”. The Horites were the original dwellers of mount Seir, before Esau came.

precepts.text: Abram pursued them unto Dan, yet the land of Dan was not established in Genesis and Israel was not even born yet; proof the scribes leave location markers for the reader.
precepts.point: They feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, as one of the royal cities, greater than Ai, and all the men thereof were mighty. So the five kings of the Amorites, the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon, gathered themselves, went up with all their hosts, and made war against Gibeon, because it had made peace with Joshua and with the children of Israel.

note.label: Joshua 10: The Day the Sun Stood Still

precepts.why:
“Adoni–zedek king of Jerusalem had heard how Joshua had taken Ai”. You might be confused why it says Jerusalem, since Jerusalem had not been set up as of yet because the land was not conquered. When the scribes wrote the history they left identifying location markers, so the reader knows visually where this is taking place.

Genesis proves it: “And when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them unto Dan.” Abram pursued them unto Dan, yet the land of Dan was not established in Genesis and Israel was not even born yet. The scribes leave location markers for the reader, and that is why the king of the Amorites is called the king of Jerusalem here.
